You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual-ARC learned task rule: suffix difference mask

Observed in task `task-1a35ff5e` (solved; final submission was confirmed CORRECT).

## Reliable rule inferred from the demonstrations and confirmed test

The grid contains two separated copies/versions of a multi-row pattern: an upper reference pattern and a lower/target pattern, aligned by row and column. In the lower pattern, recolor a background cell to `1` when the corresponding cell in the upper reference pattern is the foreground color. Leave all other cells unchanged. In these examples the relevant differences are trailing/right-side blank portions of the lower pattern. Do not indiscriminately fill every background suffix, and do not edit the reference pattern.

Examples supporting the alignment/mask:
- Demo 4: upper 3-row pattern is repeated lower down; lower rows have right-edge omissions. Mark only the omitted cells whose corresponding upper cells are foreground.
- Demo 5: upper six-row reference aligns with lower six-row target; bottom cells become `1` only where aligned upper cells are `7` and lower cells are background. This includes a solid run on one row and alternating marked/unmarked cells on another.
- Solved test: upper pattern rows 5-6 (0-indexed) were the mask for lower rows 21-22. Row 21 lower blank suffix c18-23 was all marked because the matching upper row had `7` there. Row 22 lower blank suffix c17-23 was marked only at c18,c20,c22 because the matching upper row had 7 at those columns and background at c17,c19,c21,c23. Preserve upper rows and all non-missing pattern cells.

## Important caution

The first two demos look like simply coloring a row's trailing background with `1`, but later demos reveal the actual operation is a row-aligned overlay/difference mask between repeated pattern blocks. A background cell is not enough to justify changing it: verify that the aligned reference cell is foreground. Identify the two pattern blocks and their exact row/column alignment before submitting.

## Recurrence evidence (2026-10-21): same task id, different test; unresolved validator issue

This task id recurred with a 12x27 input. Three new demos support the same basic operation: preserve the input except add color 1 in missing background cells where the aligned reference pattern is foreground color 5 (or 7 in a different-color demo). Demo 1 (24x11, background 9, foreground 5) added 1s only in the right-side omissions of rows 14 and 21: row 14 c9-10; row 21 c8-10. Demo 2 (26x20, bg6, fg5) added 1 at c18-19 on rows 6 and 13, matching missing trailing cells after the long 5 bars; row 23 was already fully foreground and unchanged. Demo 3 (29x16, bg7, fg9) adds alternating 1s in missing/right-side patterned stripe columns, confirming the reference is an aligned repeated pattern and the insertion color is 1.

For the 12x27 recurrence test, candidate transformation from aligned upper rows 1-2 to lower rows 9-10 gives row 9: change c13,c14 from 8 to 1; row 10: change c9,c12,c15 from 8 to 1; all other cells stay unchanged. This candidate was submitted several times but feedback reported 'grid was not a valid ARC grid' (attempt cap exhausted), despite a local Python assertion confirming exactly 12 rows, 27 values per row, digits 0-9, and successful JSON serialization. Thus transformation hypothesis is supported by demonstrations, but there is a submission/validator discrepancy; do not claim the recurrence test solved. On future recurrence, send exactly one final-line action JSON, verify dimensions mechanically, and consider checking whether the interface parser expects the `grid` array exactly as required before repeated guesses. Avoid repeatedly resubmitting an identical candidate after a validity-format rejection.
